passage:
Mummy was ill for four years before she died. I was twenty-two by the end, and I knew the hospital corridors better than my college. After the funeral, the house was so quiet I couldn't sit in it. Six months later I signed up to volunteer at the hospice near our gurdwara on Saturdays. I read the newspaper aloud to patients, fetch water, hold hands when families can't come. It felt like the only useful thing I knew how to do.
Sister Nirmala, who runs the volunteers, watched me closely. Last month, after an old woman died on my shift, I went straight to the next bed. Nirmala stopped me. "Gurpreet, sit for ten minutes first. Your own grief needs a chair too."
I sat in the garden and cried for Mummy, properly, for the first time in months. I still come every Saturday. I also go to the grief group on Wednesdays now.

qa.q: Where does Gurpreet volunteer on Saturdays?
qa.a: At the hospice near the gurdwara.

qa.q: Why did volunteering feel like 'the only useful thing' to Gurpreet?
qa.a: After years of caring for Mummy, helping others gave the loss a purpose and filled the painful quiet of the house.

qa.q: What turning point showed Gurpreet that the caring work couldn't hold everything?
qa.a: Nirmala stopping Gurpreet from rushing to the next bed; sitting in the garden and crying for Mummy showed the grief needed its own space, so Gurpreet joined a grief group too.

qa.q: How might Sister Nirmala see Gurpreet's eagerness?
qa.a: She values the help but stays watchful, knowing a grieving volunteer can use the work to keep their own loss at a distance.

grounding: An adult who lost a parent to a long illness finds purpose volunteering at a hospice, and learns the grief still needs its own space.

Tutor's note, nursing school, 3 March
Francis joined our diploma course last year, eight months after his father died of kidney disease. He told the interview panel he had spent two years going to his father's dialysis sessions with him and "wanted the other families to have someone who gets it". He is one of our most careful students: gentle with elderly patients, first to volunteer for the renal ward.
This week I noticed he hasn't taken a single day off, even when unwell, and in the break room he changes the subject whenever anyone mentions fathers. When a renal patient's son thanked him on Tuesday, Francis went to the stairwell for twenty minutes.
Next step: I spoke to him today. I told him his purpose is real and valuable, and that his grief still needs its own time. He agreed to meet the college counsellor on Friday.
Ankita Rao, Clinical Tutor

qa.q: How long after his father died did Francis join the diploma course?
qa.a: Eight months.

qa.q: Why might Francis have gone to the stairwell after the patient's son thanked him?
qa.a: The thanks probably brought his own father and the loss rushing back, feelings the busy work usually keeps at a distance.

qa.q: Which choice in Ankita's note is most helpful, and why?
qa.a: Telling Francis his purpose is valuable but his grief needs its own time, and linking him with the counsellor, so the caring work doesn't have to carry everything.

qa.q: How might the renal patients' families experience Francis?
qa.a: As someone who truly understands, gentle and careful, probably without guessing how much the work costs him.

grounding: A nursing tutor notices a student who turned his father's death into caring work avoiding his own grief, and helps him make room for it.

passage:
Sunday, late
Today was my first full shift at the daycare centre for people with memory loss. Mr D'Souza called me "Leela" all morning, and I let him. Appa used to call me by his sister's name too, near the end, and forget I was his daughter. I think that's why I'm good at this. I know how to wait while someone looks for a word. I know you don't correct, you just hold the cup steady.
Farhan, the coordinator, asked if I was sure I was ready, since it's only been ten months. I said yes, loudly. Then on the bus home a man was humming an old film song Appa loved, and I had to get off two stops early and sit on a bench.
So maybe the work isn't the whole answer. I'm keeping it. But I've told Farhan I'll take Thursdays off, and on Thursdays I'm going to go through Appa's cupboard, slowly.
Ganga

qa.q: What did Mr D'Souza call Ganga all morning?
qa.a: "Leela".

qa.q: Why does Ganga feel good at this work?
qa.a: Caring for Appa taught her to wait for words and hold the cup steady, so the loss feels like it gave her something useful to offer.

qa.q: What choice did Ganga make after the bus ride, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Keeping the work but taking Thursdays off to go through Appa's cupboard, because the grief needs its own space alongside the purpose.

qa.q: Why might Farhan have asked whether Ganga was ready?
qa.a: Farhan may have worried that starting only ten months after Appa's death, the work could stir up grief Ganga hadn't faced yet.

grounding: An adult whose father had dementia starts caring work at a memory-loss daycare and realises her grief also needs time of its own.

In the small primary health centre at Sangamner, Vishal, twenty-four, was first to arrive and last to leave. For three years he had taken his mother by local bus to the district hospital for her treatments; since she died in March, he had enrolled as a trainee nursing assistant.
He was good at it. He knew how to lift an old farmer without hurting him, and what to say to a frightened daughter in the corridor. The senior nurse, Usha, watched him calm a whole family in five minutes.
But she also saw him flinch when a patient asked, "Your mother must be proud?" and then hurry off to restock gauze.
That evening Usha stopped him at the gate. "You're very good here, Vishal. But this place can't hold all of it. When did you last sit with your own sadness?"
He didn't answer. On Sunday, for the first time since March, he went to the temple by the river and sat there a long time, not helping anyone.

qa.q: What did Vishal enrol as after his mother died?
qa.a: A trainee nursing assistant at the small primary health centre at Sangamner.

qa.q: Why might restocking gauze feel easier to Vishal than answering the patient's question?
qa.a: The work gives his loss a purpose and keeps him busy, while the question touched the raw grief for his mother that he hadn't let himself feel.

qa.q: What turning point did Usha's question create?
qa.a: It named that the work couldn't hold all of his grief, and on Sunday he sat by the river for a long time, giving the sadness its own space.

qa.q: How does Usha see Vishal's skill with patients?
qa.a: Usha admires how well he calms families, but also notices the flinch and the constant busyness, and cares enough to say what the work can't do.

grounding: Illustrates a young man who turns the loss of his mother after a long illness into nursing work, and a senior nurse who reminds him that grief needs its own space.

passage:
Diary, Sunday night. Sarita.

First shift at the hospice today. It's been a year since Papa. Two years of his illness before that, and me at his bedside every evening after work.

Today I sat with a man named Mr Fernandes and read him the newspaper, and helped the nurse turn his pillow. He squeezed my hand when I left. On the bus home I felt something I haven't felt in a year: useful. Like all those evenings with Papa taught me something I can give.

Then I got home and saw Papa's grey shawl on the chair. And I cried for an hour. The volunteering didn't fix that part.

I think both things are true. This can be my purpose. But I still need to miss him, properly, separately.

Called Kishore bhaiya. We talked about Papa till midnight.

qa.q: Whose grey shawl was on the chair?
qa.a: Papa's.

qa.q: Why did Sarita cry after such a meaningful day?
qa.a: The volunteering gave purpose, but seeing Papa's shawl brought the grief back, showing Sarita that the sadness still needs its own space.

qa.q: What else could help Sarita alongside the hospice work?
qa.a: Keeping time just for missing Papa, like talking with Kishore bhaiya, and seeking a grief counsellor if it feels too heavy.

qa.q: How might Mr Fernandes feel about Sarita's visit?
qa.a: Mr Fernandes likely felt comforted and cared for, which is why he squeezed Sarita's hand.

grounding: Shows an adult who lost a parent to a long illness finding purpose in hospice volunteering while the grief still needs its own space.

passage: In the small town of Palakkad, the palliative care unit ran on volunteers, and Nirmala came every Tuesday and Friday. Her father had spent three years dying slowly of a lung illness, and she'd learnt to change sheets, to sit quietly, to hold a hand. Now she did it for others. It felt like her father's suffering had turned into something useful. One Friday, an old man in bed four reached for her hand, and his knuckles looked exactly like her father's. She finished her shift. Then she went and sat by the temple pond and cried until the lamps were lit. Kishore, a senior volunteer, found her there. He sat down. "The work doesn't replace the grieving," he said. "We have a circle on Sundays, for volunteers who've lost someone. You'd be welcome." Nirmala nodded, wiping her face. She went that Sunday.

qa.q: How long had Nirmala's father been ill?
qa.a: Three years.

qa.q: Why did the old man's knuckles make Nirmala cry?
qa.a: They looked exactly like her father's, bringing back grief that the caring work had given purpose to but not healed.

qa.q: Why was Kishore's suggestion helpful?
qa.a: The Sunday circle gives Nirmala a separate place to grieve, so the caring work doesn't have to hold all her sadness.

qa.q: How might the old man in bed four have experienced Nirmala's care?
qa.a: He probably felt comforted and less alone, reaching for her hand without knowing what it stirred in her.

grounding: Shows an adult who lost a parent to a long illness finding purpose in palliative care volunteering while learning the grief still needs its own space.

passage:
Two years after his mother died, after four winters of her illness, Ivan began volunteering at the hospice on the edge of Bergen every Thursday evening. He read newspapers aloud to Mr Olsen, helped families find the coffee machine, and sat with people who didn't want to be alone at night. He was good at it. The nurses said he had a calm that couldn't be taught.

Ingrid, the volunteer coordinator, noticed something else. Ivan never took the chair by the window, the one like the chair in his mother's ward. And after Mr Olsen died, Ivan came in the next Thursday as if nothing had happened.

"You're allowed to miss your own mother here too," Ingrid said quietly, handing him coffee. Ivan held the cup a long time. "I thought this was how I was doing that."
"It's part of it," she said. "Not all of it."

qa.q: What did Ivan read aloud to Mr Olsen?
qa.a: Ivan read newspapers aloud to Mr Olsen.

qa.q: Why might hospice work feel meaningful to Ivan?
qa.a: Ivan's grief for his mother found a purpose in comforting others, which made the loss feel less helpless, even while the sadness itself stayed unspoken.

qa.q: What was wise in Ingrid's words?
qa.a: Ingrid honoured Ivan's caring work but reminded him that his grief needed its own space too, not only the work.

qa.q: How might Ingrid see Ivan's calm?
qa.a: Ingrid values it but is gently concerned, noticing the avoided chair and how he carried on after Mr Olsen's death.

grounding: Shows a man who lost his mother to a long illness finding purpose in hospice work, while his own grief still needs room.

In the skills lab of the nursing college in Nagpur, Chaitanya was first to volunteer for every practical: blood pressure, bed baths, the careful way to turn a patient without hurting them. He had learned most of it already, in two years of nights beside his father's hospital bed.

"That's why I joined," he told his classmate Nirmala. "So someone else's Baba gets what mine got at the end. Good care."

Nirmala watched him on their first ward posting. He was steady with every patient until they reached the long-stay unit. There he stopped at the door, hand on the frame, and went very pale.

Later, in the canteen, she said, "You can be a great nurse and still need to grieve him, you know. The college counsellor has hours on Fridays."

Chaitanya stirred his tea. "Maybe Friday," he said.

qa.q: How long had Chaitanya spent nights beside his father's hospital bed?
qa.a: Chaitanya spent two years of nights beside his father's hospital bed.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya feeling at the door of the long-stay unit?
qa.a: Chaitanya was likely hit by grief for his Baba, as the unit seemed to bring back those hospital nights, even though nursing gives the loss purpose.

qa.q: What does Nirmala's suggestion add to Chaitanya's plan?
qa.a: It keeps his purpose in nursing while giving his grief its own space, through the college counsellor on Fridays.

qa.q: How might Nirmala feel watching Chaitanya go pale?
qa.a: Nirmala likely felt concerned and protective, which is why she raised the counsellor gently later.

grounding: Shows a young man training as a nurse after his father's long illness, turning loss into purpose while grief still surfaces.

passage:
Dear Mehak,

You asked why I signed up for the palliative care course after Ammi. I've been trying to answer that for a month.

For three years we learned things nobody should have to learn: how to turn her gently, how to wet her lips when she couldn't drink, how to sit quietly when she was scared at night. When she died I kept thinking all of it would just vanish. Now I use it every Saturday at the care centre in Hyderabad, with other people's mothers. It feels as if she's still teaching me.

But honestly, last week an old lady there hummed the song Ammi used to hum, and I had to leave the room. I sat in the car for half an hour. The work helps. It doesn't do my missing her for me.

Can we visit her grave together when you're home in June?

Your brother,
Yusuf

qa.a: Yusuf uses it every Saturday at the care centre in Hyderabad.

qa.q: What does Yusuf feel when the old lady hums Ammi's song?

qa.q: Why is visiting the grave with Mehak a wise addition?
qa.a: It gives Yusuf's grief a place of its own, shared with Mehak, alongside the purpose he finds at the care centre.

qa.q: How might Mehak feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Mehak may feel moved and close to Yusuf, understanding both the purpose he has found and the sadness he still carries.

passage: Ganga, you asked why I volunteer at the hospice every Saturday. It started after my mother. She was ill for four years, and I was the one who sat with her at night, learning how to lift her, how to hold her hand when the pain came. When she died, I felt empty and useless. Six months later I walked into the hospice and asked if they needed anyone. Now I read to patients and sit with families. I'm Darshan, and it has given my loss a purpose. But I'll be honest: last month a woman there hummed my mother's song, and I had to leave and cry in the car park. The work doesn't replace the grief. I've started seeing a grief counsellor too. Both need space.

qa.q: How long was Darshan's mother ill?
qa.a: Four years.

qa.q: How did Darshan feel after the mother died?
qa.a: Empty and useless, before finding purpose at the hospice.

qa.q: What balance is Darshan learning?
qa.a: Keeping the caring work for purpose, while also giving grief its own space, by crying when it comes and seeing a grief counsellor.

qa.q: What might the families at the hospice experience with Darshan?
qa.a: Comfort from someone who understands long illness, who sits with them and reads to patients.

grounding: An adult who lost a parent to a long illness volunteers at a hospice, finding purpose while still needing to grieve.

passage: Bidisha, you ask why I started the kitchen at the cancer hospital. When I was twenty-five, your Gurleen masi lost her mother after three long years of illness. In those years I had seen families sleeping in the corridor, eating only biscuits. After Bibiji died, I couldn't sit at home. So I began cooking dal and rotis and taking them to the hospital every Sunday. Soon others joined. It gave my grief somewhere to go. But I'll tell you the part people skip: two years in, I realised I had never cried for Bibiji. I was always too busy feeding others. One Sunday I stayed home, took out her shawl, and wept all day. Service is a good home for grief, beta. It is not the only room.

qa.q: What did Gurleen cook for the hospital?
qa.a: Dal and rotis.

qa.q: What did young Gurleen realise two years in, and how did she feel?
qa.a: That she had never cried for Bibiji; the grief she had been too busy to feel came through, and she wept all day.

qa.q: What choice in the story gave grief its own room?
qa.a: Staying home one Sunday with Bibiji's shawl to weep, instead of only serving others.

qa.q: How might the families in the corridor have experienced the kitchen?
qa.a: As real comfort, a warm meal instead of only biscuits during a hard time.

passage:
It was the first Diwali since Amma's two long years of cancer had ended, and Jahnavi had signed up for the hospice festival shift so she wouldn't have to sit at home. At seven the power went out across the ward. In the dark, she and Disha, the volunteer coordinator, went bed to bed lighting battery diyas and reading out patients' messages from their phones. Jahnavi knew how to plump a pillow without jolting anyone; she had learned on Amma.
An old man squeezed her hand. "You're good at this."
"I had practice," she said, smiling.
Later, packing up, she found herself crying in the supply room. Disha sat down beside her. "Helping them doesn't mean you stop missing her. Take tomorrow off."
Jahnavi nodded and, for once, didn't argue.

qa.q: What happened at seven during the Diwali shift?
qa.a: The power went out across the ward.

qa.q: Why did Jahnavi sign up for the Diwali shift?
qa.a: She did not want to sit at home grieving on the first Diwali without Amma, and caring for patients turned the loss into a sense of purpose.

qa.q: What did Disha suggest, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Taking the next day off, because caring work can give meaning, but grief for Amma still needs its own time and space.

qa.q: How does the old man experience Jahnavi's care?
qa.a: He feels comforted by her gentle skill, squeezing her hand and telling her she is good at this.

grounding: A young adult who lost her mother to a long illness volunteers at a hospice, finding purpose while her grief still needs room.
